Page 01
1. What Is Shell Scripting?
Shell · Terminal · Bash · And Why DevOps Engineers Script
Shell vs Terminal vs Bash
TERMINAL — The application you open. A text interface to interact with the computer.
SHELL — The program that interprets your commands and talks to the OS.
BASH — The most common shell on Linux. "Bourne Again SHell". Command language + scripting interpreter.
What a Shell Actually Does
1Reads your command.
2Parses (understands) the command.
3Expands variables, wildcards, and paths.
4Executes the command or program.
5Returns the output and exit status.
6Waits for the next command.
User → Shell → Kernel → Output
Why DevOps Engineers Automate with Scripts
  • Save time and reduce manual work.
  • Eliminate human errors.
  • Ensure repeatability and consistency.
  • Scale operations easily.
  • Automate deployments, monitoring, backups.
  • Integrate with CI/CD pipelines.
  • Improve reliability and speed.
Interactive Commands vs Scripts
Interactive CommandsScripts
You type and run one command at a time.You write commands in a file and run them.
Used for ad-hoc tasks.Used for automation.
Hard to repeat.Repeatable and consistent.
Not version controlled.Version controlled (Git).
Easy to forget commands.Easy to share and reuse.
Your First Bash Script
hello.sh
#!/bin/bash
# This is my first script
echo "Hello, DevOps Engineer!"
DATE=$(date)
echo "Today is: $DATE"
Shebang tells the system to use Bash · Comment is ignored · echo prints to screen · $(date) stores current date in a variable.
Running a Script Safely
1Create the file
nano myscript.sh
2Save and exit
CTRL + O, ENTER, CTRL + X
3Make it executable
chmod +x myscript.sh
4Run the script
./myscript.sh
Best Practices
  • Review your script before running.
  • Use full paths for important commands.
  • Test in a safe environment first.
Important Note A script has the same power as the user who runs it. Always review scripts before executing — especially scripts downloaded from the internet.

3. Creating & Running Shell Scripts
Turn commands into automation — .sh files · Shebang · chmod · Run · Permissions · Debugging · Best Practices
1. Create .sh Files
Create a new file with .sh extension. Use any text editor: nano, vim, code. Write your commands inside. 
$ nano myscript.sh
2. The Shebang #!/bin/bash
The first line of your script should be the shebang. It tells the system to use Bash to run the script. Always use this at the top! 
#!/bin/bash
3. Make It Executable
By default, scripts are not executable. Give execute permission with chmod. 
$ chmod +x myscript.sh
4. Run Your Script
Method 1 (Recommended)
$ ./myscript.sh
Method 2
$ bash myscript.sh
Tip: Use ./ when running from the current directory.
5. File Permissions
PermSymNumMeaning
Readr4Read the file
Writew2Modify the file
Executex1Run the file
Example: -rwxr-xr--
Owner · Group · Others
Check with: ls -l myscript.sh
6. Common "Permission Denied" Errors
  • Script is not executable.
  • Wrong file permissions.
  • Trying to run without ./
  • Script has Windows line endings (CRLF).
  • Script saved with wrong ownership.
Fix: chmod +x myscript.sh
7. Debugging a Script That Won't Execute
ProblemWhy It HappensHow to Fix
Permission deniedFile is not executable or wrong permissions.chmod +x
ls -l file.sh
Command not foundShebang missing/wrong, or command doesn't exist.Check first line: #!/bin/bash
Use full path to command.
No such file or directoryWrong path or filename.Check spelling: ls -l
pwd
^M: bad interpreterWindows line endings (CRLF) in the script.sed -i 's/\r$//' f.sh
Runs but nothing happensNo execute commands or logic errors.Add set -x at top.
bash -x myscript.sh
8. Best Practices
  • Always start with #!/bin/bash
  • Make your script executable.
  • Use full paths for important commands.
  • Add comments to explain your code.
  • Test your script step by step.
  • Use set -e to exit on error.
  • Keep scripts simple and readable.
  • Great scripts start with good habits!
Remember: Great scripts start with good habits!

2. Shell Commands You Must Know First
Navigate · Create · View · Paths · Combine · Read · Practice
1. Navigate Your File System
pwdPrint working directory · pwd → /home/user
lsList files and folders · ls → file1.txt docs images
cd [dir]Change directory · cd docs (moves into docs)
cd ..Go up one directory · cd .. (moves up one level)
cd ~Go to your home directory · cd ~ → /home/user
2. Create, Copy, Move, Delete
mkdir [dir]Create a new directory · mkdir new_folder
touch [file]Create an empty file · touch notes.txt
cp [src] [dest]Copy files or folders · cp file1.txt backup.txt
mv [src] [dest]Move or rename files/folders · mv old.txt new.txt
rm [file]Remove (delete) files · rm temp.txt
3. View File Content
cat [file]Display entire file · cat notes.txt
less [file]View file page by page · less largefile.log
head [file]Show first 10 lines · head file.log
tail [file]Show last 10 lines · tail file.log
4. Absolute vs Relative Paths
ABSOLUTE PATH (full from root)
/home/user/docs/file.txt
  • Starts from the root /
  • Always points to the correct location
RELATIVE PATH (based on current location)
Current: /home/user
docs/file.txt
  • Does not start with /
  • Depends on where you are
5. Combining Commands
;Run commands one after another · mkdir test ; cd test ; touch file.txt
&&Run next only if first succeeds · mkdir test && cd test
||Run next if first fails · mkdir test || echo "Failed"
|Send output to another command · ls -l | less
>Redirect output (overwrite) · ls > output.txt
>>Redirect output (append) · echo "Hi" >> notes.txt
6. Reading Command Output
ls -l Lists files in long format.
ls -l | less Sends output to less so you can scroll.
cat file.txt | head -n 5 Shows first 5 lines of a file.
grep "error" app.log Searches for the word "error".

5. Reading User Input & Script Arguments
Get input · Use arguments · Build smarter scripts
read · $1 $2 $3 · $# · $@
1. read: Get User Input
Use read to get input from the user.
input.sh
read -p "Enter your name: " NAME
echo "Hello, $NAME"
-p shows a prompt. The value is stored in the variable.
2. Script Arguments
Pass values to a script when you run it.
SymbolMeaningExample
$0Script name./deploy.sh
$1First argumentdev
$2Second argumentus-east-1
$3Third argumentapp1
$#Number of arguments3
$@All arguments"$@"
3. Passing Arguments
Run your script with values. 
$ ./deploy.sh dev us-east-1 app1
Inside the script:
$1 = dev
$2 = us-east-1
$3 = app1
4. Validating Arguments
Always check if arguments are provided. 
if [ $# -lt 3 ]; then
  echo "Usage: $0 <env> <region> <app>"
  exit 1
fi
Prevents errors and confusion.
5. Common Practices
  • Always validate arguments.
  • Use meaningful names.
  • Quote "$@" when using all args.
  • Give helpful usage messages.
  • Exit with code 1 on error.
6. Example: Simple Reusable DevOps Script
deploy.sh
#!/bin/bash
# Check arguments
if [ $# -lt 3 ]; then
  echo "Usage: $0 <env> <region> <app>"
  exit 1
fi

# Assign arguments to variables
ENV=$1
REGION=$2
APP=$3

# Use variables
echo "Environment: $ENV"
echo "Region: $REGION"
echo "Application: $APP"
echo "Deploying $APP to $ENV in $REGION..."
Run Example
$ ./deploy.sh dev us-east-1 app1
Environment: dev
Region: us-east-1
Application: app1
Deploying app1 to dev in us-east-1...
What This Script Does
1Checks if 3 arguments are provided.
2Assigns values to variables.
3Prints the values.
4Ready to add real DevOps tasks.
Tip: Good scripts take input, validate it, and do useful work. That's the foundation of automation!

4. Variables and Environment Variables

Store data. Reuse. Automate.
1. Creating Variables
  • No spaces around = sign.
NAME=DevOps COUNT=5
2. Reading Variables
  • Use $ to read a variable.
echo $NAME
Output: DevOps
3. Quoting Variables
  • Use quotes to handle spaces.
  • Prevents word splitting.
  • Prevents filename expansion.
echo "$NAME" echo '$NAME'
4. Command Substitution
  • Store the output of a command.
DATE=$(date +%Y-%m-%d) echo $DATE
Output: 2025-05-18
5. Export Variables
  • Makes a variable available to child processes.
  • Use export.
export PROJECT=MyApp echo $PROJECT
Output: MyApp
6. Environment Variables
  • Set by the system.
  • Available in every shell.
bash
echo $HOME echo $USER echo $SHELL echo $LANG
HOME
Your home directory.
echo $HOME
Output: /home/user
USER
Current logged-in user.
echo $USER
Output: user
PATH
Directories where commands are searched.
echo $PATH
Output: /usr/bin:/bin:/usr/local/bin
8. Using Variables in Scripts
  • Make your scripts flexible and powerful.
bash
#!/bin/bash APP_NAME="MyApp" LOG_DIR="$HOME/logs" mkdir -p "$LOG_DIR" echo "Starting $APP_NAME...." echo "Logs will be saved in $LOG_DIR"
9. Best Practices
  • Always use quotes when in doubt.
  • Use meaningful variable names.
  • Export only what you need.
  • Keep variables uppercase for constants.
  • Use command substitution $( ) often.
  • Test your scripts with different values.
TIP: Variables are the foundation of flexible scripts. Quote strings, name clearly, export only what you need.

6. Exit Codes and Command Success

Every command returns a status.
1. What Exit Codes Mean

After any command runs, the system returns a number called an exit code. It tells you if the command succeeded or failed.

echo $?
Shows the exit code of the last command.
2. Basic Exit Code Rules
0
Exit Code 0 · Success
Command completed successfully.
1+
Non-zero · Failure
Something went wrong. Check the error.
3a. Valid Path
ls /home
echo $?
Output: 0
3b. Missing Path
ls /notfoundfolder
echo $?
Output: 2
3c. Read File
cat file.txt
echo $?
Output: 0 or 1+
4. The exit Command
  • Use exit to end a script and return a code.
  • exit 0 = success
  • exit 1 = failure
  • Ends the script with a status.
bash
if [ ! -f file.txt ]; then echo "File not found!" exit 1 fi
5. Testing Command Success
  • Use exit codes in conditions.
bash
ls /home if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then echo "Success" else echo "Failed" fi
$? -eq 0 Success$? -ne 0 Failure
6. Why CI/CD Depends on Exit Codes
  • Each step returns an exit code.
  • CI/CD tools stop the pipeline on failure.
  • 0 = pipeline continues.
  • 1+ = pipeline fails.
  • Ensures reliable and consistent deployments.
Play→Gear→Check
7. Preventing Silent Automation Failures
  • Always check exit codes. Don't ignore command results.
  • Use set -e. Stops the script on first failure.
  • Log errors clearly. Makes debugging much easier.
  • Validate inputs before running. Bad inputs cause unexpected failures.
  • Test your scripts regularly. Catches issues early.
TIP: Never ignore exit codes. Check them, handle them, and your scripts will be reliable and safe.

7. Conditional Statements

Make smart decisions in your scripts.
1. Basic Syntax
if [ condition ]; then commands elif [ condition ]; then commands else commands fi
ifStart conditionthenRun if trueelifElse if another conditionelseRun if all falsefiEnd condition
2. Numeric Comparisons
OpMeaning
-eqEqual
-neNot equal
-gtGreater than
-ltLess than
-geGreater or equal
-leLess or equal
if [ $a -eq $b ]
3. String Comparisons
OpMeaning
=Equal
!=Not equal
-zString is empty
-nString not empty
if [ "$a" = "$b" ]
Note: Always quote strings! Prevents errors with spaces.
4. File Tests
OpMeaning
-fFile exists
-dDirectory exists
-eFile or dir exists
-rReadable
-wWritable
-xExecutable
-sFile is not empty
if [ -f file.txt ]
5a. Check File
bash
if [ -f /etc/passwd ]; then echo "File exists" else echo "File not found" fi
5b. Check Directory
bash
if [ -d /var/log ]; then echo "Directory exists" else echo "Directory not found" fi
5c. Check Service
bash
if systemctl is-active --quiet nginx; then echo "Nginx is running" else echo "Nginx is not running" fi
6. Practical Example
Check disk space and act based on the result.
bash
USAGE=$(df / | awk 'NR==2 {print $5}' | tr -d '%') if [ "$USAGE" -gt 80 ]; then echo "Disk usage is high: ${USAGE}%" elif [ "$USAGE" -gt 60 ]; then echo "Disk usage is moderate: ${USAGE}%" else echo "Disk usage is normal: ${USAGE}%" fi
7. Quick Reference
  • if Start condition
  • then Run if true
  • elif Else if
  • else Run if all false
  • fi End condition
  • Use spaces inside [ ].
  • Quote strings.
  • Use numeric operators without quotes.
  • Test before you act.
  • Make scripts smart and reliable.
TIP: Conditions make your scripts intelligent. Always test, validate, and handle every situation.

8. Logical Operators and Multiple Conditions

Combine tests. Make smarter decisions.
1. Logical Operators
OperatorMeaningExampleDescription
&&ANDif [ $a -gt 5 ] && [ $b -lt 10 ]Both conditions must be true.
||ORif [ $a -gt 5 ] || [ $b -lt 10 ]At least one condition must be true.
!NOTif ! [ -f file.txt ]Reverses the result.
2. Short-Circuit Execution
&&
AND
If the first condition is false, the second is NOT executed.
||
OR
If the first condition is true, the second is NOT executed.
!
NOT
Flips true to false, and false to true.
Insight: Saves time and prevents unnecessary checks.
3. AND (&&)
  • Both conditions must be true.
bash
if [ -f app.sh ] && [ -x app.sh ]; then echo "File exists and is executable" else echo "Check failed" fi
Use for strict requirements.
4. OR (||)
  • At least one condition must be true.
bash
if [ -f app.sh ] || [ -f app.py ]; then echo "Script found" else echo "No script found" fi
Use for alternatives.
5. NOT (!)
  • Reverse a condition.
bash
if [ ! -f config.env ]; then echo "Config file missing" else echo "Config file exists" fi
Use to detect missing items.
6. Combining Multiple Tests
You can mix &&, ||, and ! for powerful checks.
Example 1: Mix AND & OR
bash
if [ -f deploy.sh ] && [ -x deploy.sh ] || [ -f deploy.py ]; then echo "Ready to deploy" else echo "Deployment script missing" fi
➔ Executable deploy.sh OR deploy.py exists.
Example 2: Negation + AND
bash
if [ ! -f .lock ] && [ -d /var/log ]; then echo "Safe to proceed" else echo "Lock exists or log dir missing" fi
➔ No lock file AND directory exists.
Example 3: Complex
bash
if [ -f app.conf ] && [ -r app.conf ] && ! [ -z "$1" ]; then echo "All checks passed" else echo "Validation failed" fi
➔ File exists, readable AND $1 not empty.
7. Building Safer Deployment Checks
Example: Before deploying, validate everything.
bash
if [ -f app.tar.gz ] && [ -s app.tar.gz ] && [ -x /usr/bin/docker ] && ! systemctl is-active --quiet app; then echo "All checks passed. Starting deployment..." # Your deployment commands here else echo "Deployment aborted. Check requirements." exit 1 fi
Deployment Checklist
  • File exists AND not empty.
  • Docker is installed.
  • App service is not running.
  • Proceed only when everything is correct.
  • Prevents failed or risky deployments.
SAFE DEPLOYMENT STARTS HERE!
TIP: Combine checks, validate early, and fail fast. Smart conditions = reliable automation.

9. Loops for Automation

Repeat tasks. Save time. Eliminate manual work.
1. For Loops
  • Loop through a list of items.
bash
for item in a b c; do echo "Item: $item" done
Output: Item: a Item: b Item: c
3. Looping Through Files
  • Process each file in a directory.
bash
for file in *.txt; do echo "File: $file" done
Prints all .txt files in the current directory.
5. Break
  • Exit the loop immediately.
STOP THE LOOP
bash
for i in {1..5}; do if [ $i -eq 3 ]; then break fi echo "Number: $i" done
Output: Number: 1 Number: 2
7. Avoiding Infinite Loops
  • Always update your condition.
  • Always change the variable inside the loop.
  • Use clear exit conditions.
  • Test your loops with small values first.
  • Use break when needed.
BE CAREFUL
2. While Loops
  • Repeat while a condition is true.
bash
count=1 while [ $count -le 5 ]; do echo "Count: $count" count=$((count + 1)) done
Output: Count: 1 2 3 4 5
4. Looping Through Servers
  • Run commands on multiple servers.
bash
for server in server1 server2 server3; do echo "Checking $server..." ssh $server uptime done
Check uptime on many servers.
6. Continue
  • Skip the rest of the loop and continue.
SKIP AND CONTINUE
bash
for i in {1..5}; do if [ $i -eq 3 ]; then continue fi echo "Number: $i" done
Output: Number: 1 2 4 5
8. Automating Repetitive Tasks
Loops help you automate daily tasks:
  • File management
  • Server monitoring
  • User management
  • Log analysis
  • Backups and cleanups
  • System updates
AUTOMATE EVERYTHING
KEY TAKEAWAY: Loops save time, reduce errors, and make your scripts powerful.
REPEAT SMARTER · SAVE TIME EVERY DAY

10.FUNCTIONS AND REUSABLE SCRIPTS

Write once. Use many times. Stay organized.
1CREATING FUNCTIONS

Define a function using a name and () block.

functions.sh
greet() {{ echo "Hello, DevOps Engineer!" }}
2CALLING FUNCTIONS

Call the function by its name.

call.sh
$ greet Hello, DevOps Engineer!
3FUNCTION ARGUMENTS

Pass values to functions.

args.sh
greet_user() {{ echo "Hello, $1!" }} greet_user "Ann" Hello, Ann!

Keep variables private to the function.

local.sh
calculate() {{ local num=10 echo "Inside: $num" }} calculate echo "Outside: $num" Inside: 10 Outside:
5RETURN STATUS

Functions return an exit status.

return.sh
check_disk() {{ if [ $1 -gt 80 ]; then return 1 else return 0 fi }} check_disk 90 echo "Status: $?" Status: 1
6BREAK LARGE SCRIPTS

Make scripts smaller, cleaner, and easier to read.

  • check_system()
  • backup_files()
  • deploy_app()
  • send_alert()
  • cleanup()
  • print_summary()
7REUSABLE AUTOMATION PATTERNS
  • Health checks
  • Log rotations
  • Backups
  • User management
  • Deployments
  • System cleanups
8KEEP SCRIPTS MAINTAINABLE
  • Use meaningful function names.
  • Keep functions small and focused.
  • Add comments to explain purpose.
  • Test each function before using it.
  • Reuse functions across scripts.
Key TakeawayFunctions make scripts powerful, reusable, and easy to maintain.
Build OnceUse Many Times

11.WORKING WITH FILES AND DIRECTORIES

Organize. Protect. Automate.
1CHECKING WHETHER FILES EXIST

Use -f for files, -d for directories.

check.sh
if [ -f file.txt ]; then echo "File exists" fi if [ -d mydir ]; then echo "Directory exists" fi

Create only if it does not exist.

3COPYING AND MOVING FILES

Copy files or directories.

cp.sh
cp file.txt /backup/ cp -r mydir /backup/

Move or rename files.

mv.sh
mv old.txt new.txt mv file.txt /archive/
4SEARCHING FOR FILES

Find files by name.

find-name.sh
find /home/user -name "*.log"

Search by type.

find-type.sh
find /var/log -type f -name "*.log"
5FILE PERMISSIONS

View permissions.

ls-l.sh
ls -l file.txt

Change permissions.

chmod.sh
chmod 644 file.txt chmod +x script.sh
6DISK USAGE CHECKS

Check disk usage.

df.sh
df -h

Check folder size.

du.sh

7CLEANING TEMPORARY FILES

Remove files older than 7 days.

rm.sh

8BUILDING A SIMPLE BACKUP SCRIPT

Example: Backup a folder.

backup.sh
#!/bin/bash SOURCE="/home/user/data" DEST="/backup" DATE=$(date +%F) tar -czf "$DEST/backup-$DATE.tar.gz" "$SOURCE" echo "Backup completed: backup-$DATE.tar.gz"

13.REDIRECTION, PIPES, AND LOGS

Control output. Capture logs. Debug smarter.
1STANDARD INPUT (STDIN)

Input from keyboard or file.

stdin.sh
command < file.txt sort < names.txt
2STANDARD OUTPUT (STDOUT)

Normal command output.

stdout.sh
ls -l echo "Hello"
3STANDARD ERROR (STDERR)

Error messages and warnings.

stderr.sh
ls no_file cat no_file.txt
4OUTPUT REDIRECTION

Overwrite output to a file.

bash
command > file.log
OVERWRITE FILE
5APPEND REDIRECTION

Append output to a file.

bash
command >> file.log
APPEND TO FILE
6ERROR REDIRECTION

Redirect errors to a file.

bash
command 2> error.log
ERRORS ONLY
7COMBINE STDOUT & STDERR

Send both output and errors to same file.

bash
command > output.log 2>&1
OUTPUT + ERRORS TOGETHER
8PIPES (|)

Send output of one command as input to another.

bash
ps aux | grep nginx | wc -l
FILTER AND PROCESS DATA
9SEND OUTPUT TO LOG FILES

Log everything for monitoring and audits.

log-all.sh
#!/bin/bash echo "Starting script..." > script.log ls -l /var/log >> script.log df -h >> script.log echo "Script completed." >> script.log
LOG FILE
10CAPTURING ERRORS SEPARATELY

Keep success and errors in different files.

split-logs.sh
#!/bin/bash command > success.log 2> error.log echo "Done" >> success.log
SUCCESS.LOG
ERROR.LOG
11COMMON EXAMPLES
  • ls -l > files.txt — Save output to file (overwrite)
  • ls -l >> files.txt — Append output to file
  • command 2> error.log — Save errors to error.log
  • command > all.log 2>&1 — Output + errors to all.log
  • command | grep "pattern" — Filter output using grep
  • cat access.log | grep 404 | wc -l — Count 404 errors

Log outputs

Capture important output for audits.

Separate errors

Keep stderr apart from stdout.

Use append

>> for long-running logs.

Use pipes

Analyze data on the fly.

Check logs

Always verify and rotate them.

14.PROCESSES AND SERVICES

Monitor. Control. Keep everything running.
1PS – VIEW PROCESSES

Show running processes.

Useful columns:

  • PID – Process ID
  • USER – Owner
  • %CPU, %MEM – Usage
  • COMMAND – Process name
2PGREP – FIND PROCESSES

Find process IDs by name.

pgrep.sh

Used for scripting and automation.

3KILL – STOP PROCESSES

Stop processes using PID.

kill.sh
kill 1234 kill -9 1234
  • kill – graceful (SIGTERM)
  • kill -9 – force (SIGKILL)
Use kill -9 only when needed.
4SYSTEMCTL – MANAGE SERVICES

Control system services (Linux).

systemctl.sh
systemctl start nginx systemctl stop nginx systemctl restart nginx systemctl enable nginx

Works with systemd services.

5CHECK IF PROCESS RUNNING

Check if a process is running.

check-proc.sh
pgrep nginx >/dev/null if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then echo "Running" else echo "Not running" fi

Exit code 0 = running

6CHECK SERVICE STATUS

Check status of a service.

status.sh
systemctl status nginx

Common states:

  • ● active (running)
  • ● inactive (dead)
  • ! failed
7RESTART FAILED SERVICES

Restart a service.

restart.sh
systemctl restart nginx systemctl enable nginx systemctl status nginx

Auto-restart on boot + check again.

8PROCESS INFORMATION

Get more details about a process.

ps-info.sh

Show parent process with ppid.

9BASIC SERVICE HEALTH CHECK

Example: Check and restart service.

health.sh
#!/bin/bash SERVICE=nginx pgrep $SERVICE >/dev/null if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then echo "$SERVICE is running" else echo "$SERVICE is down. Restarting..." systemctl restart $SERVICE fi

16. ERROR HANDLING & SAFER SCRIPTS

WRITE PREDICTABLE. RELIABLE. SAFE AUTOMATION.
Page 16 of 20
1. WHY SCRIPTS FAIL SILENTLY

By default, bash ignores errors and keeps going — hiding real issues.

{terminal('rm file.txt\necho "Deleted"\necho "Script finished"', 'bad.sh')} {callout('Problem: If rm fails, the script keeps running and hides the error.', 'danger', 'bug')}
2. SET -E: EXIT ON ERROR

Exit immediately if any command fails.

{terminal('set -e\nrm file.txt\n# runs only if rm succeeds', 'set -e')} {callout('Benefit: Stops the script when a command fails.', 'tip', 'check-circle')}
3. SET -U: UNSET VARS

Exit if you use a variable that is not set.

{terminal('set -u\necho "$UNSET_VAR"\n# fails fast', 'set -u')} {callout('Benefit: Catches typos and missing variables early.', 'tip', 'check-circle')}
4. SET -O PIPEFAIL

Detect failures inside pipelines.

{terminal('set -o pipefail\ncat file | grep "ERR" | wc -l', 'pipefail')} {callout('Benefit: Without pipefail, only the last command\'s status is checked.', 'tip', 'check-circle')}
5. SET -EUO PIPEFAIL

Best practice for safer scripts.

{terminal('set -euo pipefail', 'safe-mode')}
  • Exit on any command error
  • Error on unset variables
  • Catch pipeline failures

WRITE SAFER. SLEEP BETTER.

6. VALIDATING INPUTS

Always verify inputs before using them.

{terminal('if [ -z "$1" ]; then\n echo "Usage: $0 <url>"\n exit 1\nfi', 'validate')} {callout('Benefit: Prevents errors; makes scripts user-friendly.', 'tip', 'check-circle')}
7. CHECK DEPENDENCIES

Ensure required commands exist before running.

{terminal('if ! command -v curl >/dev/null 2>&1; then\n echo "curl not found!"\n exit 1\nfi', 'dep-check')} {callout('Benefit: Avoids failures due to missing tools.', 'tip', 'check-circle')}
8. HANDLING FAILURES

Check command results and handle failures.

{terminal('if ! rm file.txt; then\n echo "Failed to remove file.txt"\n exit 1\nfi', 'handle')} {callout('Benefit: React to failures; prevent bad outcomes.', 'tip', 'check-circle')}
9. CLEAN UP ON FAIL

Use traps to clean up on exit or error.

{terminal('cleanup() {{\n echo "Cleaning up..."\n rm -f temp.log\n}}\ntrap cleanup EXIT', 'trap')} {callout('Benefit: Keeps systems clean even when scripts fail.', 'tip', 'check-circle')}
10. PREDICTABLE AUTOMATION

Follow these rules for reliable scripts:

  • Fail fast
  • Validate inputs
  • Check dependencies
  • Handle errors
  • Clean up properly
  • Log what happens
  • Exit with the right status code

Result: Reliable and predictable automation every time.

11. SAFETY CHECKLIST

The 7 rules of safer scripts:

  • Use set -euo pipefail
  • Validate all user inputs
  • Check command dependencies
  • Handle command failures
  • Trap cleanup on EXIT
  • Log every action
  • Exit 0 / non-zero explicitly
12. WHY IT MATTERS

Safe scripts = Less downtime, fewer bugs, happier users.

Always handle errors. Always clean up. Always be predictable.

EXAMPLE: SAFE SCRIPT TEMPLATE

safe-template.sh
#!/bin/bash\nset -euo pipefail\n\n# Check input\nif [ -z "$1" ]; then\n echo "Usage: $0 <url>"; exit 1\nfi\n\n# Check dependency\ncommand -v curl >/dev/null 2>&1 || {{ echo "curl not found"; exit 1; }}\n\n# Cleanup trap\ncleanup() {{ echo "Cleaning up..."; rm -f temp.log; }}\ntrap cleanup EXIT\n\n# Main logic\nURL="$1"\nHTTP_CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{{http_code}}" "$URL")\nif [ "$HTTP_CODE" -ge 200 ] && [ "$HTTP_CODE" -lt 400 ]; then\n echo "[$URL] is UP (HTTP $HTTP_CODE)"\nelse\n echo "[$URL] is DOWN (HTTP $HTTP_CODE)"; exit 1\nfi
Safe Mode — set -euo pipefail makes the script strict and safe.
Validate Input — Ensure the user provides the required input.
Check Dependency — Stop early if a required tool is missing.
Cleanup on Exit — Cleanup runs automatically on success or failure.
Main Logic — Do the work and check results.
Exit Status — Exit 0 for success, non-zero for failure.
KEY TAKEAWAYSafe scripts = less downtime, fewer bugs, and happier users. Always handle errors. Always clean up. Always be predictable.

avail.sh
#!/bin/bash\nURL="https://example.com"\nSTATUS=$(curl -so /dev/null -w "%{{http_code}}" "$URL")\nif [ "$STATUS" = "200" ]; then\n echo "[OK] $URL is UP (200)"\nelse\n echo "[DOWN] $URL is DOWN (Code: $STATUS)"\nfi

18. SCHEDULING SCRIPTS WITH CRON

AUTOMATE TASKS. SAVE TIME. STAY RELIABLE.

1. WHAT CRON DOES

Cron runs commands or scripts automatically at scheduled times. Perfect for backups, cleanup, monitoring, reports, and more.

2. UNDERSTANDING CRONTAB

Crontab is your personal cron schedule.

crontab
crontab -e # Edit\ncrontab -l # List jobs\ncrontab -r # Remove all jobs

3. CRON TIMING SYNTAX

Five fields: MIN HOUR DAY MONTH DOW

FieldRange
MIN0–59
HOUR0–23
DAY1–31
MONTH1–12
DOW0–6 (0=Sun)

EXAMPLES

PatternMeaning
* * * * *Every minute
0 * * * *Every hour at :00
0 2 * * *Daily at 2 AM
30 1 * * 1Mon at 1:30 AM
0 3 1 * *1st of month at 3 AM

4. RUNNING SCRIPTS AUTOMATICALLY

Add your cron job with crontab -e. Cron runs jobs in the background — no need to keep your terminal open. Great for hands-off automation.

5. ENVIRONMENT DIFFERENCES

Cron runs with a minimal environment. Your PATH, variables, and shell may be different. Use full paths in scripts and set needed variables inside the script.

env
PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin\nexport PATH

6. LOGGING CRON OUTPUT

Always log output for debugging. Redirect output and errors.

logging
*/5 * * * * /path/to/script.sh \\n >> /var/log/mycron.log 2>&1

7. COMMON CRON FAILURES

Watch for these pitfalls:

  • Wrong timing syntax
  • Script path incorrect
  • Script not executable
  • Missing environment variables
  • No permissions to run script
  • Output not logged
  • Mail not configured
  • Cron service not running

8. BACKUP & CLEANUP JOBS

Two practical scheduled-job examples:

jobs
# BACKUP JOB — daily at 2 AM\n0 2 * * * /backup.sh \>> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1\n\n# CLEANUP JOB — weekly Sun at 3:30 AM\n30 3 * * 0 /cleanup.sh \>> /var/log/cleanup.log 2>&1

,Values list (1,2,3)
-Range (1-5)

0-23Hour

1-12Month
0-6Day of week (0=Sun)
@dailySame as 0 0 * * *
@weeklySame as 0 0 * * 0
@rebootRun once at startup
BEST PRACTICES
  • Use full paths for commands and scripts.
  • Log all cron outputs.
  • Test scripts manually before scheduling.
  • Keep cron jobs simple and reliable.
  • Review your crontab regularly.
  • Set PATH and needed variables inside scripts.
  • Make scripts executable (chmod +x).

17. DEBUGGING SHELL SCRIPTS

FIND ISSUES. UNDERSTAND CAUSES. FIX FAST.
Page 19 of 20

1. READING SHELL ERRORS

Errors tell you what went wrong. Read them carefully — the message always gives a clue.

bash
./script.sh: line 10: mycmd: command not found\n./script.sh: line 15: [ : : integer expression expected\nPermission denied\nNo such file or directory
Tip: The error message always gives a clue. Look at the line number and message.

2. DEBUG MODE WITH BASH -X

Run your script with bash -x to see each command as it executes.

bash
$ bash -x script.sh\n# Example output:\n+ echo "Starting"\nStarting\n+ VAR=hello\n+ echo $VAR\nhello\n+ ls /not/exist\nls: cannot access '/not/exist': No such file or directory

3. DEBUG MODE INSIDE SCRIPT

Use set -x to enable debug inside the script.

bash
set -x\n# Your commands here\nset +x # Turn off debug
Benefit: Shows each command as it runs. Very helpful to trace issues.

4. COMMON PROBLEMS & FIXES

Six common failure categories:

A. SYNTAX ERRORS

Missing symbols or wrong structure.

if [ "${VAR}" = "x" ] echo "missing fi"

Fix: check brackets, then/fi, do/done.

B. QUOTING PROBLEMS

Wrong quotes break the script.

echo "Hi $USER" # ok echo 'Hi $USER' # literal echo "He said "hi"" # bad

Fix: use double quotes; escape inner.

C. MISSING VARIABLES

Using variables that are not set.

echo $NAME ./script.sh: line 5: NAME: unbound variable

Fix: define or use ${NAME:-default}.

D. PERMISSION ERRORS

Script or files not executable.

./script.sh: line 3: ./other.sh: Permission denied

Fix: chmod +x script.sh.

E. PATH PROBLEMS

Command not found.

mycmd: command not found

Fix: check PATH or use full path.

F. FILE MISSING

File or directory does not exist.

cat: file.txt: No such file or directory

Fix: verify path; use absolute path.

5. DEBUGGING STEP BY STEP

A repeatable workflow for fixing any script:

1. Read the error — Understand what the error says. Note the line number and message.
2. Reproduce the issue — Run the script and confirm the error happens again.
3. Run with bash -x — Use bash -x script.sh to see each command and where it fails.
4. Check variables and quotes — Make sure variables are set and quoted correctly.
5. Fix and test again — Make the change and run again. Repeat until the error is gone.
6. Remove debug — Remove set -x or stop using bash -x after fixing.
COMMON ERROR MESSAGES

What each message usually means:

  • command not found — PATH issue or typo.
  • Permission denied — missing +x or wrong owner.
  • No such file — path typo or missing file.
  • unbound variable — used with set -u.
  • integer expression expected — non-numeric in [ ].
  • unexpected token — missing fi, done, or quote.
DEBUG TOOLBOX

Tools to debug shell scripts:

ToolUse
bash -xTrace each command
set -x / set +xToggle trace
bash -vVerbose (read lines)
bash -nSyntax check only
shellcheckStatic linter
echo $VARInspect value
trapCatch signals/errors
DEBUG CHECKLIST
  • Read the error message.
  • Reproduce consistently.
  • Trace with bash -x.
  • Verify all variables.
  • Check all quotes.
  • Confirm file paths exist.
  • Validate permissions.
  • Test fix; remove debug.
KEY TAKEAWAYRead errors carefully, reproduce the issue, and trace with bash -x. Most bugs are syntax, quoting, or path issues. Debug methodically — don't guess.
